The problem I see with this half-glass-full take, at least when it comes to employees, is that when a given % of your workflow is automated or made redundant via AI, that efficiency gain is not viewed as augmentation, nor does it result into doing more of "the parts you like." It's leveraged by your employer, who now sees a process that required 5 people can be done by 3, can get the same or more output for less money and from fewer people, and adjusts accordingly to maximize gains. If you think I'm exaggerating, ask anyone who worked a corporate job 30-40 years ago. Did the proliferation of PCs and the elimination of communication lag/blackouts brought on by mobile phones result in you doing more of what you like? No. Secretaries and administrative assistants became redundant and a luxury of the few, employee tracking became more strict to maximize productivity. Executives now had to inherit their secretaries' greatly-simplified workload, and the productivity gains from the widespread adoption of that technology went straight to the top while the quality of life of the remaining employees went down. Rather than floating all boats, these gains benefited few. Now, AI can take some of that inherited workload off your hands again, free up time... and we're somehow to assume it won't just result in tighter deadlines and adjusted requirements to squeeze every ounce of productivity out of you? Unless the benefits of all this technology trickle down more aggressively, you'll just see growth at the top, stagnation in the narrowing middle, and more and more people falling off the wagon.
